findings.topic: Vultr Serverless Inference: base URL, OpenAI compatibility, endpoints (verified)
findings.detail: The team outline is correct. The base URL is https://api.vultrinference.com/v1 and the API is OpenAI-compatible. Chat goes to POST https://api.vultrinference.com/v1/chat/completions, with body fields model, messages, max_tokens and optional tools / tool_choice ("auto" | "required" | "none") (https://docs.vultr.com/products/compute/serverless-inference/management/usage/chat.md). Vultr's Python guide uses the stock OpenAI SDK: openai.OpenAI(api_key=os.environ.get('VULTR_SERVERLESS_INFERENCE_API_KEY'), base_url="https://api.vultrinference.com/v1") (https://docs.vultr.com/how-to-use-vultr-serverless-inference-in-python). I checked live at 01:34 ET today. GET /v1/models returns the model catalogue with no auth. An unauthenticated POST /v1/chat/completions returns HTTP 401 {"error":{"code":401,"message":"No API key provided","type":"auth_error"}}, so the endpoint is up.
findings.recommendation: Hard-code nothing except the default base URL in config. Call it with httpx (already a FastAPI dependency) or the openai SDK with base_url overridden. Read the model id from an env var so a model swap needs no code change.

findings.topic: Auth header and how to get the inference key
findings.detail: Inference calls use 'Authorization: Bearer ${INFERENCE_API_KEY}'. This is the subscription's own key, separate from the account-level Vultr API key, which is used only for management calls to https://api.vultr.com/v2 (https://docs.vultr.com/products/compute/serverless-inference/management/usage/chat.md). Create a subscription in one of three ways: (1) Console: Products > Serverless > Inference > Add Serverless Inference, enter a Label, accept the models list and charges note. (2) API: POST https://api.vultr.com/v2/inference with body {"label":"stillhere"}. (3) CLI: vultr-cli inference create --label stillhere (https://docs.vultr.com/products/compute/serverless-inference/provisioning). Get the key from the console Overview page, from GET https://api.vultr.com/v2/inference/{inference-id}, or with vultr-cli inference get <id> (https://docs.vultr.com/products/compute/serverless-inference/management/connection.md). The JSON field is api_key (https://docs.vultr.com/reference/terraform/data-sources/inference.md).
findings.recommendation: Use the console path tonight (about 1 minute). Put the key in .env as VULTR_INFERENCE_API_KEY. Never commit it, because the scaffold goes straight to main.

findings.topic: Available models (live catalogue, 17 Oct 2026)
findings.detail:
Text-output chat models from GET https://api.vultrinference.com/v1/models, priced in USD per 1M tokens (input / output):
- qwen3.8-flash-next: 0.10 / 0.20, 262K context, Seattle
- glm-5.3-flash: 0.10 / 0.35, 1M context
- mimo-v2.6-flash-rl: 0.10 / 0.25
- nemotron-3-nano-omni-30b-a3b-reasoning: 0.10 / 0.25
- deepseek-v4.1-flash: 0.15 / 0.60
- qwen3.8-27b: 0.15 / 1.00
- minimax-m3: 0.20 / 0.90
- muse-glimmer-30b: 0.25 / 1.00
- glm-5.x-menthol: 0.40 / 1.75
- mimo-v2.6-pro-rl: 0.40 / 0.80
- glm-5.2 and glm-5.3: 0.75 / 3.00
- nemotron-3.5-content-safety: 0.05 / 0.15 (a moderation classifier)

Other types: qwen3-embedding-4b (embeddings), bge-reranker-v2-m3 and vultron-retriever-* (rerank), whisper-large-v3-turbo (speech to text), qwen3-tts-12hz-1.7b (text to speech), z-image-turbo and minimax-h3 (image/video), clef and clef-flash (decision models). All chat models except the content-safety model list 'tools', 'response_format' and 'structured_outputs' among their supported parameters. The docs say tool calling works only on kimi-k2-instruct (https://docs.vultr.com/products/compute/serverless-inference/management/usage/chat.md), but that model is no longer in the live list, so that note is out of date. Vultr's FAQ also says to check the console model selector for the current list (https://docs.vultr.com/products/serverless/inference/faq).
findings.recommendation: Default LLM_MODEL=qwen3.8-flash-next: cheapest, fast, supports JSON response_format. Fall back to glm-5.3-flash. You could run nemotron-3.5-content-safety over generated text as a second check, but a local banned-phrase filter is enough. Keep the model id in an env var, because the docs' kimi-k2-instruct example has already rotted.

findings.topic: Pricing / billing model (sources conflict)
findings.detail:
The sources disagree on pricing:
- The live /v1/models catalogue gives a separate per-token price for each model (see the previous finding) (https://api.vultrinference.com/v1/models).
- A Vultr support doc updated 10 Mar 2026 says Serverless Inference is billed by tokens at $0.55 per 1M input and $2.75 per 1M output, and calls it a 'subscription'. It also says usage is tracked in the console Usage tab (https://docs.vultr.com/support/products/serverless/how-do-i-monitor-the-usage-and-cost-of-my-vultr-serverless-inference-subscription).
- The older vultr.com product page, seen only through search because vultr.com returns 403 to fetchers, advertised $10/month for 50,000,000 tokens plus $0.0002 per 1K tokens overage (https://www.vultr.com/products/cloud-inference/).
- The provisioning flow makes you acknowledge a 'charges note' (https://docs.vultr.com/products/compute/serverless-inference/provisioning).

Even at the highest rate ($0.55 in / $2.75 out), one explanation of about 600 input + 150 output tokens costs about $0.0007, so 1,000 calls cost under $1. That is my arithmetic, not a Vultr figure.
findings.recommendation: Read the charges note in the console when you create the subscription. If it shows a flat $10/month fee, the $100 MLH credit covers it. Cap max_tokens at about 300. Delete the subscription after judging.

findings.topic: Rate limits
findings.detail: Vultr publishes no rate limits for Serverless Inference. The FAQ index has no rate-limit article (https://docs.vultr.com/support/products/serverless), and the live responses I checked carry no x-ratelimit headers (server: 'FrankenPHP Caddy'). The only documented Vultr limit is for the management API: requests are counted per source IP, and above 30 requests/second you may get HTTP 429 (https://docs.vultr.com/support/platform/api/what-rate-limits-apply-to-the-vultr-api).
findings.recommendation:
Treat the LLM as best-effort:
- Set an httpx timeout of about 6 s.
- On 429 or 5xx, retry once with jittered backoff.
- After that, fall back to the deterministic template.
- Cache one explanation per flag event so judges refreshing the page don't re-call the API.

findings.topic: Data handling (privacy rubric: 10 pts)
findings.detail: Vultr says inference data is processed in memory and 'not stored persistently by default', is protected by TLS in transit, and needs an API key. The page does not say whether prompts are used for training, and it does not cover logging (https://docs.vultr.com/support/products/serverless/how-secure-is-my-data-using-vultr-serverless-inference, updated 15 Apr 2026).
findings.recommendation: Send the LLM only derived, non-identifying factors, for example {"missed_checkins":2,"hr_delta_bpm":+34,"head_tilt_s":40,"pulled_forward_by":"hr"}. Never send names, phone numbers, Telegram ids or location. Location stays in Postgres and is released only at alert time, as in your design. Say this explicitly in the privacy section of the pitch.

findings.topic: MLH x Vultr credit: amount and steps
findings.detail:
MLH's partner page gives $100 in Vultr credit. The steps are:
1. Register at mlh.link/vultr-discover, which redirects to https://discover.vultr.com/mlh. Use your school name as Company and 'Student' as Job Title.
2. Verify the registration email.
3. Sign up at mlh.link/vultr-signup (https://www.vultr.com/register/).
4. Enter the promo code in the Gift Code field under Billing.

MLH notes that multiple registrations are not allowed (https://www.mlh.com/partners/vultr). The short link mlh.link/vultr-giftcode redirects to https://my.vultr.com/billing/?promo=HACKATHON (I resolved it with curl). Vultr's own MLH page says 'Every hacker gets free Vultr credit to use during their event' (https://discover.vultr.com/mlh). Vultr allows one promo code per user, and promo credits expire and cannot be transferred (https://docs.vultr.com/support/platform/billing/how-can-i-add-a-promotional-code).
findings.recommendation: One teammate should do this now, before building anything else, because email and payment verification are the slowest part. Ask the HTV MLH coach to confirm the code.

findings.topic: Does the credit need a credit card or other payment method?
findings.detail: Yes. Vultr's billing FAQ says 'A valid Credit Card or PayPal must be linked to register for services and be eligible for promotions - one promo per user', and that PayPal needs a backup funding source such as a card or bank account (https://docs.vultr.com/platform/billing/faq.md). The promo-code page repeats that a credit card or PayPal must be linked (https://docs.vultr.com/support/platform/billing/how-can-i-add-a-promotional-code). The account-creation guide says you land on Billing after signup. There you can choose 'I just want to link my credit card - $0.00 deposit', which may place a temporary authorization hold; other payment methods need a small deposit (https://docs.vultr.com/platform/create-an-account.md). Accepted methods are credit and debit cards, BitPay, PayPal and Alipay, and they are verified before you can provision anything (https://docs.vultr.com/support/platform/billing/why-do-i-need-to-enter-a-payment-method). A web-search summary claimed MLH says 'no credit card required', but the MLH page text I pulled does not say that (https://www.mlh.com/partners/vultr).
findings.recommendation: Plan for a card or PayPal: one teammate links a card using the $0.00 option. If nobody can, drop the Vultr track rather than burn time. The backend runs fine locally and on Tiger Cloud without Vultr. Destroy the instance and the inference subscription after judging to avoid charges once credits run out.

findings.topic: Best Use of Vultr prize: what judges look for
findings.detail: On other MLH events' prize pages, the Vultr category asks hackers to sign up for a Vultr account, claim free cloud credits, and 'Take your next hack to the cloud with Vultr'. No formal list of products that count is published (https://www.mlh.com/events/hackcmu/prizes). I could not find a Hack the Valley 11 prize page to confirm the HTV-specific wording.
findings.recommendation:
Use Vultr twice so it is clearly load-bearing and easy to see in the demo:
- Host the live API, worker and judge QR page on Vultr Cloud Compute.
- Generate the 'why it flagged' explanation with Vultr Serverless Inference.

Show the public https URL and a /healthz endpoint that reports llm=vultr. Check the HTV Devpost for the exact prize text.

findings.topic: Cloud Compute: region, plan, image IDs
findings.detail:
Region: the public Vultr API lists yto (Toronto) as the only Canadian region (https://api.vultr.com/v2/regions). It is the nearest to Tiger Cloud ca-central-1.

Plans available in yto, from https://api.vultr.com/v2/plans?type=vc2:
- vc2-1c-1gb: 1 vCPU / 1 GB / 25 GB, $5/month, $0.007/hour
- vc2-1c-2gb: $10/month, $0.014/hour
- vc2-2c-2gb: $15/month, $0.021/hour

Images, from https://api.vultr.com/v2/os and https://api.vultr.com/v2/applications:
- Ubuntu 24.04 LTS x64: os id 2284
- Marketplace app 'Docker on Ubuntu 24.04': app id 1125, image_id 'docker'

Vultr's Docker app guide says the install can take up to 10 minutes after boot. It does not say Compose is preinstalled; it installs a standalone docker-compose binary instead. It suggests 1 GB / 1 CPU for testing (https://docs.vultr.com/how-to-use-vultrs-docker-marketplace-application). Docker's convenience script (curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh) installs docker-ce together with docker-compose-plugin and supports Ubuntu 24.04. Docker says the script is not recommended for production (https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/).
findings.recommendation: Use plain Ubuntu 24.04 (os 2284) plus a cloud-init script that runs get.docker.com. That gives you the 'docker compose' v2 plugin and avoids the marketplace image's 10-minute install and missing Compose. Pick vc2-1c-2gb in yto: building a Python image on 1 GB can run out of memory (my judgment).

findings.topic: Cloud-init (user data)
findings.detail:
In the console, go to Additional Features, tick 'Enable Cloud-Init User-Data' and paste the script. Scripts run as root on first boot only. Logs are at /var/log/cloud-init.log and /var/log/cloud-init-output.log (https://docs.vultr.com/how-to-deploy-a-vultr-server-with-cloudinit-userdata/). The CLI accepts --userdata or --userdata-file, plus --region, --plan, --os or --app, --ssh-keys, --firewall-group, --host and --label (https://docs.vultr.com/reference/vultr-cli/instance/create.md).

Suggested user data:
#!/bin/bash
set -euxo pipefail
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git /opt/stillhere

CLI equivalent:
vultr-cli instance create --region yto --plan vc2-1c-2gb --os 2284 --label stillhere --ssh-keys <KEY_ID> --firewall-group <FW_ID> --userdata-file cloud-init.sh

Then copy .env over with scp and run: cd /opt/stillhere && docker compose --profile vultr up -d --build
findings.recommendation: Keep secrets out of user data: DATABASE_URL, the Telegram token and VULTR_INFERENCE_API_KEY go into .env, copied over with scp after boot. If something fails, check /var/log/cloud-init-output.log first.

findings.topic: Firewall ports
findings.detail: Vultr Firewall groups filter incoming traffic by protocol, port and source (https://docs.vultr.com/products/network/firewall/management/rules). The Terraform rule fields are protocol, ip_type, subnet, subnet_size and port. To attach a group, either PATCH https://api.vultr.com/v2/instances/{instance-id} with {"firewall_group_id":"<id>"} or run vultr-cli instance update-firewall-group --instance-id <id> --firewall-group-id <id> (https://docs.vultr.com/products/compute/instances/cloud-compute/networking/enable-firewall.md). Docker-published ports bypass ufw: 'traffic to and from that container gets diverted before it goes through the ufw firewall settings' (https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/packet-filtering-firewalls/). Whether ufw is on by default on Vultr images varies; check with sudo ufw status verbose (https://docs.vultr.com/firewall-quickstart-for-vultr-cloud-servers/).
findings.recommendation: Create a Vultr Firewall group (outside the VM, so Docker can't bypass it) that allows only TCP 22 (ideally from your IP), 80 and 443. In compose, publish the API as 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 so only Caddy can reach it. Don't publish the worker or any database port. Tiger Cloud is reached outbound.

findings.topic: HTTPS with Caddy, no domain needed
findings.detail: Caddy issues certificates automatically when the hostname's A/AAAA record points to the server and ports 80 and 443 are reachable (https://caddyserver.com/docs/automatic-https). The one-line reverse proxy is: caddy reverse-proxy --from example.com --to :9000 (https://caddyserver.com/docs/quick-starts/reverse-proxy). Use the official caddy:2 image and persist /data, where certificates and keys are stored (https://hub.docker.com/_/caddy). Without a domain, use nip.io: 64-176-22-9.nip.io resolves to 64.176.22.9, Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 works with it, and Let's Encrypt raised the nip.io/sslip.io limit to 250,000 certificates (https://nip.io/). Fallback: Let's Encrypt has issued 6-day IP-address certificates under the 'shortlived' profile since 15 Jan 2026 (https://letsencrypt.org/2026/01/15/6day-and-ip-general-availability.html).
findings.recommendation: Set PUBLIC_HOSTNAME=stillhere.<ip-with-dashes>.nip.io. Caddy service: image caddy:2, profiles [vultr], command 'caddy reverse-proxy --from ${PUBLIC_HOSTNAME} --to api:8000', ports 80:80 and 443:443, volumes caddy_data:/data and caddy_config:/config. The judge QR code points at https://${PUBLIC_HOSTNAME}/c/<token>. Web Bluetooth needs a secure context, so serve the Chrome HeartCast page from this HTTPS host or localhost.

findings.topic: Rough time to first deploy
findings.detail: Vultr's docs don't give a general provisioning time; the VX1 page says 'ready for use in seconds' (https://docs.vultr.com/vultr-vx1-cloud-compute). An independent benchmark measured Vultr at a median of 78 s, range 30 to 260 s (https://vpsbenchmarks.com/hosters/vultr). The Docker marketplace app adds up to 10 minutes (https://docs.vultr.com/how-to-use-vultrs-docker-marketplace-application).
findings.recommendation:
My estimate if the repo already builds locally:
- Signup, card link and promo: 5–10 min
- Inference key: 2 min
- Instance: 1–2 min
- get.docker.com: about 2–4 min
- Build, start, and Caddy certificate: 3–5 min

That is about 20–30 minutes; budget 45–60 minutes with debugging. Deploy a hello-world /healthz first, before the escalation logic is finished.

findings.topic: How the scaffold should integrate Vultr and still run locally without it
findings.detail:
Every Vultr piece is optional and gated by env vars, and nothing in the safety path depends on it. Specific names follow.

1) Config (app/config.py, pydantic-settings):
- llm_base_url = 'https://api.vultrinference.com/v1'
- llm_api_key: str | None, from env VULTR_INFERENCE_API_KEY
- llm_model = 'qwen3.8-flash-next'
- llm_timeout_s = 6.0
- public_hostname: str | None

2) app/explain.py:
- template_explanation(factors: dict) -> str: always works, deterministic.
- async llm_explanation(factors: dict) -> str | None: POSTs {llm_base_url}/chat/completions with 'Authorization: Bearer <key>', max_tokens=300 and response_format JSON. Returns None when there is no key, on timeout, on non-2xx, or when the output contains banned phrases (spiked, drugged, unconscious, incapacitated, overdose, diagnos*).
- async explain(factors) -> {text, source: 'vultr' | 'template'}.
- The system prompt says the model may only restate the provided factors and must never infer a medical state. This matches the KAZE ban on claiming to detect spiking or incapacitation.

3) Store the explanation; never call the LLM from the escalation worker. Table:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS flag_explanations (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  checkin_id bigint NOT NULL,
  factors jsonb NOT NULL,
  text text NOT NULL,
  source text NOT NULL CHECK (source IN ('template','vultr')),
  model text,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
The worker's claim query stays pure SQL:
WITH due AS (
  SELECT id FROM checkin_timers
  WHERE status = 'armed' AND due_at <= now()
  ORDER BY due_at
  LIMIT 20
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE checkin_timers t
SET status = 'firing', claimed_at = now(), claimed_by = %(worker_id)s
FROM due WHERE t.id = due.id
RETURNING t.id, t.wearer_id, t.stage;

4) Endpoints:
- GET /healthz returns {db: ok, llm: 'vultr' | 'disabled'}.
- GET /api/checkins/{id}/why returns the deterministic factor list plus the stored text. This covers the PointClickCare 'explain why it flags' bonus and their 'use of AI' criterion.

5) docker-compose.yml: one image, three services.
- api: uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000, ports 127.0.0.1:8000:8000
- worker: python -m app.worker, restart: unless-stopped
- caddy: under profiles: ['vultr']
Locally, 'docker compose up' or plain 'uvicorn app.main:app --reload' plus 'python -m app.worker' runs with no Vultr key and no Caddy. On Vultr, run 'docker compose --profile vultr up -d --build'. DATABASE_URL points at Tiger Cloud in both cases.
findings.recommendation: Ship .env.example with VULTR_INFERENCE_API_KEY left blank. Add a pytest that runs explain() with no key and asserts source == 'template'. Make sure alert delivery (Telegram + QR page) never waits on the LLM: alerts use the template text immediately, and the LLM text, if any, attaches afterwards.

bottom_line:
Your outline's Vultr endpoint is right. https://api.vultrinference.com/v1 is OpenAI-compatible: POST /v1/chat/completions with 'Authorization: Bearer <inference key>'. That key is separate from the account API key. You get it from Console > Serverless > Inference or GET https://api.vultr.com/v2/inference/{id}, field api_key.

- **Models:** the live, unauthenticated GET /v1/models shows the current list with per-model token prices. qwen3.8-flash-next costs $0.10/$0.20 per 1M tokens and supports JSON output. The docs' kimi-k2-instruct example is out of date.
- **Pricing:** the sources disagree. The live catalogue gives per-token prices; a Mar 2026 doc says $0.55/$2.75 per 1M; an older page said $10/month for 50M tokens. Check the charges note in the console. Any of these is a few dollars at most for a hackathon.
- **Rate limits:** none are published for inference. Use a timeout, one retry, then the template fallback.
- **MLH credit:** $100. Register at discover.vultr.com/mlh, sign up, then enter the code under Billing > Gift Code. Vultr requires a linked credit card (a $0.00 link option exists) or PayPal to get promo credit, so one teammate with a card should do it now.
- **Fastest deploy tonight:** vc2-1c-2gb in Toronto (yto) on Ubuntu 24.04 (os 2284), with cloud-init running get.docker.com and cloning the repo. Copy .env over with scp, then run 'docker compose --profile vultr up -d --build'. Caddy (caddy:2) proxies to api:8000 on a <ip-dashes>.nip.io hostname for automatic HTTPS. A Vultr Firewall group allows only 22, 80 and 443; Docker-published ports bypass ufw, so bind the API to 127.0.0.1. This is roughly 20–30 minutes if the repo already builds; budget up to an hour.
- **Scaffold:** gate everything on env vars. With no VULTR_INFERENCE_API_KEY, explain() returns a deterministic template. Caddy sits behind a compose profile. The escalation worker (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) never calls the LLM. So local runs work with only DATABASE_URL, and Vultr is purely additive.

No files were created. I did not open the Google Doc link from the relayed request; this step only covered the Vultr research.

findings.topic: 0. Version baseline on Tiger Cloud (run this check first)
findings.recommendation: Put the output of the version query in the README or judge notes. All SQL below assumes TimescaleDB 2.23 or later and Toolkit 1.3 or later; a 2.30.x service meets both. If the service reports an older version, use the create_hypertable path in finding 1. Nothing in this report was run against a live database. Run each statement once on the trial service before the demo.

findings.topic: 1. Hypertable creation: CREATE TABLE ... WITH (tsdb.hypertable) vs create_hypertable
findings.detail:
Syntax: CREATE TABLE ... WITH (tsdb.hypertable, tsdb.columnstore, tsdb.partition_column, tsdb.chunk_interval, tsdb.segmentby, tsdb.orderby, tsdb.sparse_index, tsdb.create_default_indexes, tsdb.direct_compress ...).
Version requirements and defaults:
- The syntax applies from TimescaleDB 2.20.0.
- From 2.23.0 the partition column is chosen automatically, and creation errors if several timestamp columns qualify.
- tsdb.chunk_interval defaults to 7 days.
- tsdb.columnstore defaults to true and automatically creates a columnstore policy whose 'after' equals the chunk interval, with a 1-day schedule.
- tsdb.segmentby is auto-selected if you omit it.
- tsdb.orderby defaults to time descending.
- tsdb.direct_compress is a tech preview from 2.29.0.
The older path is CREATE TABLE, then SELECT create_hypertable('t', by_range('ts', INTERVAL '1 day')), then ALTER TABLE t SET (timescaledb.enable_columnstore, timescaledb.segmentby='device_id', timescaledb.orderby='ts DESC'), then CALL add_columnstore_policy(...). Sources: https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/reference/timescaledb/hypertables/create_hypertable and https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/reference/timescaledb/hypercore/alter_table.
Recommended SQL for StillHere:
CREATE TABLE accel_samples (
  ts TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  device_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  ax REAL, ay REAL, az REAL,
  pitch_deg REAL,
  source TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'live'  -- 'live' | 'synthetic'
) WITH (
  tsdb.hypertable,
  tsdb.partition_column = 'ts',
  tsdb.chunk_interval = '1 day',
  tsdb.segmentby = 'device_id',
  tsdb.orderby = 'ts DESC'
);
CREATE INDEX ON accel_samples (device_id, ts DESC);

CREATE TABLE hr_samples (
  ts TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  device_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  bpm REAL NOT NULL,
  source TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'heartcast'
) WITH (tsdb.hypertable, tsdb.partition_column = 'ts', tsdb.chunk_interval = '1 day',
        tsdb.segmentby = 'device_id', tsdb.orderby = 'ts DESC');
CREATE INDEX ON hr_samples (device_id, ts DESC);

-- Confirm the auto-created columnstore policy (after = 1 day):
SELECT job_id, hypertable_name, schedule_interval, config
FROM timescaledb_information.jobs WHERE proc_name = 'policy_compression';
findings.recommendation: Use CREATE TABLE ... WITH (tsdb.hypertable ...) because it is the current, documented one-statement path. Always set tsdb.partition_column explicitly so a second timestamp column such as received_at cannot cause an error. Keep accelerometer and heart-rate data in separate hypertables, because they arrive at very different rates. Keep the check-in timers, escalation state and contacts in plain Postgres tables, not hypertables: they are small and their rows change often, and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED needs plain row-store rows. Do not enable tsdb.direct_compress, which the docs mark 'tech preview and not production-ready'.

findings.topic: 2. Chunk interval, segmentby and orderby for ~50 Hz per device
findings.detail:
Volume: 50 rows/s × 86,400 s = 4.32 M rows per day per device.
Documented sizing rules (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/learn/hypertables/sizing-hypertable-chunks):
- Set chunk_interval 'so that the indexes of chunks currently being ingested into fit within 25% of main memory'.
- Watch for 'over 1,000 chunks in a single hypertable'.
- Very small chunks compress poorly.
Columnstore policy behaviour (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/reference/timescaledb/hypercore/add_columnstore_policy): it acts on chunks, 'Add chunks containing data older than now - {after}'. The schedule_interval defaults to 12 hours when the chunk interval is 1 day or more.
The columnstore 'is optimized for 1000 rows per batch per segmentby value' (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/build/data-management/write-data/insert). 4.32 M rows per device per day gives full batches.
A continuous aggregate's own chunk interval defaults to 10× the source chunk interval (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/use-timescale/latest/continuous-aggregates/create-a-continuous-aggregate).
Useful queries: SELECT show_chunks('accel_samples'); and SELECT show_chunks('accel_samples', older_than => INTERVAL '1 day'); (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/reference/timescaledb/hypertables/show_chunks). To change the interval later: SELECT set_chunk_time_interval('accel_samples', INTERVAL '1 day'); this affects only new chunks.
findings.recommendation:
Use chunk_interval = '1 day', segmentby = 'device_id' and orderby = 'ts DESC'. Two reasons:
- With a few devices, daily index growth is far below 25% of RAM.
- Each chunk is one day, so 'compress after 1 day' and 'drop after N days' line up with chunk boundaries and give visible results within the hackathon. With the 7-day default, nothing would be compressible before Sunday.
Do not add device_id as a space-partitioning dimension; segmentby is the right tool. If 50 Hz raw data is not needed server-side, downsampling on the bridge (for example to 10 Hz) is also a fair privacy point.

findings.topic: 3. Continuous aggregates at 1 minute -> 1 hour -> 1 day (hierarchical, cagg on cagg)
findings.detail:
Rules for stacking continuous aggregates (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/learn/continuous-aggregates/hierarchical-continuous-aggregates):
- Requires TimescaleDB 2.9.0 or later.
- The upper bucket must be at least as wide as the lower bucket and a whole multiple of it.
- A fixed-width bucket cannot sit on a month or year bucket.
- The docs pattern for the upper layer is rollup() of a Toolkit summary, for example mean(rollup(percentile_hourly)).
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW options (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/reference/timescaledb/continuous-aggregates/create_materialized_view):
- timescaledb.continuous (required).
- timescaledb.materialized_only (default TRUE).
- timescaledb.chunk_interval: renamed in 2.20, and the old chunk_time_interval name is rejected.
- timescaledb.create_group_indexes.
- WITH DATA is the default. To create the view inside a transaction block, use WITH NO DATA.
Window functions inside a cagg definition are experimental since 2.20 and off by default, so compute rolling windows at query time instead.
SQL:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW hr_1m
WITH (timescaledb.continuous, timescaledb.materialized_only = false) AS
SELECT time_bucket(INTERVAL '1 minute', ts) AS bucket, device_id,
       stats_agg(bpm) AS hr_stats,
       time_weight('Linear', ts, bpm) AS hr_tw
FROM hr_samples
GROUP BY time_bucket(INTERVAL '1 minute', ts), device_id
WITH NO DATA;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW hr_1h
WITH (timescaledb.continuous, timescaledb.materialized_only = false) AS
SELECT time_bucket(INTERVAL '1 hour', bucket) AS bucket, device_id,
       rollup(hr_stats) AS hr_stats, rollup(hr_tw) AS hr_tw
FROM hr_1m
GROUP BY time_bucket(INTERVAL '1 hour', bucket), device_id
WITH NO DATA;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW hr_1d
WITH (timescaledb.continuous, timescaledb.materialized_only = false) AS
SELECT time_bucket(INTERVAL '1 day', bucket) AS bucket, device_id,
       rollup(hr_stats) AS hr_stats, rollup(hr_tw) AS hr_tw
FROM hr_1h
GROUP BY time_bucket(INTERVAL '1 day', bucket), device_id
WITH NO DATA;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW accel_1m
WITH (timescaledb.continuous, timescaledb.materialized_only = false) AS
SELECT time_bucket(INTERVAL '1 minute', ts) AS bucket, device_id,
       stats_agg(pitch_deg) AS pitch_stats,
       stats_agg(sqrt(ax*ax + ay*ay + az*az)) AS mag_stats
FROM accel_samples
GROUP BY time_bucket(INTERVAL '1 minute', ts), device_id
WITH NO DATA;
(accel_1h and accel_1d follow the same pattern as hr_1h and hr_1d.)
findings.recommendation: Write the GROUP BY as the full time_bucket(...) expression, not the alias 'bucket'. In GROUP BY, Postgres resolves an ambiguous name to the input column, so 'GROUP BY bucket' in hr_1h would group by the 1-minute bucket. Store Toolkit summaries (stats_agg, time_weight) in the 1-minute layer, not plain avg(), so the 1h and 1d layers can rollup() exact mean, stddev and count. Buckets are UTC by default, which is fine for the demo.

findings.topic: 4. Real-time aggregation across the stack
findings.detail: Since TimescaleDB 2.13, real-time aggregation is off by default (materialized_only = true). Turn it on with ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW <name> SET (timescaledb.materialized_only = false); or set it in the CREATE WITH clause, as in finding 3. A real-time query combines the materialized rows with raw rows newer than the refresh watermark. Late data added to a bucket that is already materialized is not reflected until the next refresh or a manual refresh_continuous_aggregate (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/learn/continuous-aggregates/real-time-aggregates). In a stack, each layer sees only the layer directly below it. Unmaterialized data is joined recursively only while every layer is real-time; one materialized-only layer stops the recursion, and layers above it see only its materialized data (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/learn/continuous-aggregates/hierarchical-continuous-aggregates).
findings.recommendation: Set materialized_only = false on every layer (hr_1m, hr_1h, hr_1d and the accelerometer caggs) so that the hourly and daily views include the last minute live during judging. Check it with SELECT view_name, materialized_only FROM timescaledb_information.continuous_aggregates;. In the pitch, call this 'live rollups with incremental materialization'.

findings.topic: 5. Refresh policies, the two-bucket rule and backfill order
findings.recommendation: Run the migration script with psycopg.connect(..., autocommit=True), or with psql, because CALL refresh_... and CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WITH DATA fail inside a transaction. After a backfill, always refresh 1m, then 1h, then 1d, because each layer only sees what the layer below has materialized.

findings.topic: 6. Toolkit hyperfunctions: stats_agg, average, stddev, num_vals, rollup, rolling, time_weight
findings.detail:
Signatures from the Toolkit reference:
- stats_agg(value DOUBLE PRECISION) RETURNS StatsSummary1D. Available since Toolkit 1.3.0; a BIGINT variant also exists (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/reference/toolkit/statistical-and-regression-analysis/stats_agg-one-variable/stats_agg).
- average(summary StatsSummary1D) RETURNS DOUBLE PRECISION.
- stddev(summary StatsSummary1D, [method TEXT]). The method defaults to 'sample'; 'population' or 'pop' also work (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/reference/toolkit/statistical-and-regression-analysis/stats_agg-one-variable/stddev).
- num_vals(summary) RETURNS BIGINT.
- rollup(ss StatsSummary1D) RETURNS StatsSummary1D, for re-aggregating, for example 1h from 1m.
- rolling(ss StatsSummary1D) RETURNS StatsSummary1D, used only as a window function with OVER. The docs say it can be much faster over caggs because it uses inverse transition functions, with possible small floating-point error.
The docs rolling example contains a stray comma before FROM; remove it when copying. The overview example is: average(rolling(stats_agg(temperature)) OVER (ORDER BY time_bucket('1 day'::interval, time) ROWS 6 PRECEDING)) (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/api/latest/hyperfunctions/stats_aggs).
Time-weighted functions:
- time_weight(method TEXT, ts TIMESTAMPTZ, value DOUBLE PRECISION) RETURNS TimeWeightSummary. Available since Toolkit 1.0.0. Method is 'Linear' (alias 'trapezoidal') or 'LOCF', case-insensitive (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/reference/toolkit/time_weight/time_weight).
- average(tws TimeWeightSummary) RETURNS DOUBLE PRECISION, and rollup(tws TimeWeightSummary).
- The time-weighted average returns NULL when a bucket has a single value.
- time_weight works in continuous aggregates but is not parallelizable (https://docs.timescale.com/use-timescale/latest/hyperfunctions/time-weighted-averages/time-weighted-average).
findings.recommendation: Use stats_agg in the caggs, then average, stddev and num_vals at query time. Use rollup() for the hierarchy and rolling() for sliding baselines. Use time_weight('Linear', ...) for heart rate, because BLE heart-rate samples arrive at uneven intervals and a plain avg() over-weights bursts. For 'Best Use of Tiger Data', point out that one stats_agg column feeds mean, stddev and count at 1m, 1h and 1d, with exact merges and no raw rescans.

findings.topic: 7. Z-score of a recent window against a 7-day baseline (an explainable 'check in sooner' signal)
findings.detail:
Variant A (recommended) compares like with like: the mean of the last 5 minutes against the distribution of 1-minute means over the prior 7 days.
WITH per_min AS (
  SELECT device_id, bucket, average(hr_stats) AS bpm_1m
  FROM hr_1m
  WHERE device_id = %(device)s AND bucket >= now() - INTERVAL '7 days'
), baseline AS (
  SELECT device_id, stats_agg(bpm_1m) AS s
  FROM per_min WHERE bucket < now() - INTERVAL '15 minutes'
  GROUP BY device_id
), recent AS (
  SELECT device_id, avg(bpm_1m) AS bpm_recent, max(bucket) AS last_bucket
  FROM per_min WHERE bucket >= now() - INTERVAL '5 minutes'
  GROUP BY device_id
)
SELECT r.device_id, r.last_bucket,
  round(r.bpm_recent::numeric,1) AS recent_bpm,
  round(average(b.s)::numeric,1) AS baseline_bpm,
  round(stddev(b.s)::numeric,1) AS baseline_sd,
  num_vals(b.s) AS baseline_minutes,
  round(((r.bpm_recent - average(b.s)) / NULLIF(stddev(b.s),0))::numeric,2) AS z
FROM recent r JOIN baseline b USING (device_id);

Variant B is a rolling z-score per hour from hr_1h, using a Postgres RANGE frame with an interval offset that excludes the current hour (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-expressions.html):
SELECT bucket, device_id, average(hr_stats) AS hour_bpm,
  (average(hr_stats) - average(rolling(hr_stats) OVER w)) / NULLIF(stddev(rolling(hr_stats) OVER w),0) AS z_vs_prior_7d
FROM hr_1h
WHERE device_id = 'demo-01' AND bucket >= now() - INTERVAL '8 days'
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY bucket RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND INTERVAL '1 hour' PRECEDING)
ORDER BY bucket;
In variant B, stddev is the spread of individual samples (rollup and rolling merge exactly), so z for an hourly mean is conservative.
The same pattern works on accel_1m.pitch_stats for head-position change.
findings.recommendation: Return the components with the score: recent_bpm, baseline_bpm ± baseline_sd, baseline_minutes and z. The UI can then say, for example: 'Heart rate over the last 5 min (118) is 3.1 SD above your own 7-day baseline (74 ± 14, 9,800 min of data), so StillHere moved your next check-in earlier. No one was alerted.' This covers PointClickCare's 'explain why it flags' bonus and stays within KAZE's rules: only advance the check-in, never escalate on z, and never describe it as detecting spiking or incapacitation. Use a fixed threshold such as |z| ≥ 3 with baseline_minutes ≥ 120, and say that the baseline is synthetic during the demo.

findings.topic: 8. Columnstore (compression) policies, manual conversion for the demo, and showing the ratio
findings.recommendation: Keep the auto-created 1-day policy; there is no need to re-add it. For judging, backfill at least 2 days of synthetic accelerometer data so a full 1-day chunk is closed. Then run compress_chunk or run_job live and show the before, after and ratio row. Do not quote a ratio until you have measured it on your own data; the docs' tiny example even shows 'after' larger than 'before'.

findings.topic: 9. Columnstore + retention + continuous aggregates together: yes, under these rules
findings.recommendation: Present retention as a privacy feature for KAZE's privacy points: raw motion and heart-rate samples delete themselves after 3 days, and only per-minute summaries are kept for 14 days. Keep location out of these hypertables entirely, consistent with releasing it only at alert time. Do not run CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate('hr_1m', NULL, ...) after raw chunks have been dropped.

findings.topic: 10. Batch ingestion from Python psycopg 3: COPY vs executemany
findings.detail:
COPY in psycopg 3 uses cursor.copy('COPY t (cols) FROM STDIN') plus copy.write_row(row) inside a with block (https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/basic/copy.html).
- Binary format needs set_types(), because the server applies no casts.
- There is an async form: async with cur.copy(...) and await copy.write_row(...).
executemany() 'makes use internally of the pipeline mode' from psycopg 3.1, but COPY is not supported in pipeline mode (https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/advanced/pipeline.html).
- The cursor docs say executemany is 'Performance optimised ... when using libpq 14 or newer' and suggest copy() for many INSERTs (https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/api/cursors.html).
- Check the libpq version with psycopg.pq.version().
- pip install "psycopg[binary]" bundles the client libraries.
On Tiger Cloud, COPY ... FROM '<file>' and FROM PROGRAM are not available; use FROM STDIN. Tiger Data's own docs say COPY 'can be 2-3x faster or more than INSERT' (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/build/data-management/write-data/insert).
Vendor benchmark at 100 M rows: COPY took 316 s, batched INSERT 2,653 s and single-row INSERT 94,623 s (https://tigerdata.com/learn/testing-postgres-ingest-insert-vs-batch-insert-vs-copy). INSERT ... SELECT FROM unnest(arrays) was about 2× faster than multi-row VALUES and supports ON CONFLICT (https://tigerdata.com/blog/boosting-postgres-insert-performance).
Code:
COPY_SQL = "COPY accel_samples (ts, device_id, ax, ay, az, pitch_deg) FROM STDIN"
def flush_accel(conn, rows):  # rows: list of (aware datetime, str, float, float, float, float)
    with conn.cursor() as cur, cur.copy(COPY_SQL) as cp:
        for r in rows:
            cp.write_row(r)
    conn.commit()
# alternative
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO accel_samples (ts, device_id, ax, ay, az, pitch_deg) VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s)", rows)
# idempotent retries (needs CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON hr_samples (device_id, ts);)
cur.execute("INSERT INTO hr_samples (ts, device_id, bpm) SELECT * FROM unnest(%s::timestamptz[], %s::text[], %s::real[]) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING", (ts_list, dev_list, bpm_list))
findings.recommendation: At about 50 rows/s per device, any batched method is fast enough; the mistake to avoid is one commit per row. Buffer in bridge.py or FastAPI and flush every 1–2 s (50–100 rows per device) with text-format COPY on a long-lived connection, which gives one round trip and one commit per batch. Use the unnest + ON CONFLICT form for heart rate only if retries can resend the same samples. Skip timescaledb.skip_cagg_invalidation (2.28+), which is meant for bulk migrations, and skip direct compress.

findings.topic: 11. Showing query latency honestly (EXPLAIN ANALYZE plus client timing)
findings.detail:
How EXPLAIN works in Postgres 18 (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-explain.html):
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement. Wrap INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE in BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...; ROLLBACK;.
- In PG 18, 'Buffers information is automatically included when ANALYZE is used'.
- SUMMARY prints 'Planning Time' and 'Execution Time'.
- ANALYZE adds profiling overhead.
- SERIALIZE measures output conversion, but network transfer is never measured.
psql \timing on shows each statement's elapsed time in ms (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-psql.html). pg_stat_statements, which is on by default on Tiger Cloud, exposes mean_exec_time and max_exec_time (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgstatstatements.html).
Tiger Console Monitoring > Insights shows the median or P95 per query, a 'Columnar tables' flag, and buffer hit/miss. It only captures EXPLAIN plans automatically for queries over 10 s, and new queries take a few minutes to appear (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/deploy/tiger-cloud/tiger-cloud-aws/monitoring).
Plan node names depend on version: compressed chunks appear as 'Custom Scan (ColumnarScan)', renamed from DecompressChunk in 2.22.0, and DeferredChunkAppend is new in 2.30.0 (https://github.com/timescale/timescaledb/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
Demo SQL (raw scan vs cagg, same answer):
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', ts) h, avg(bpm) FROM hr_samples
WHERE device_id = 'demo-01' AND ts > now() - INTERVAL '3 days' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT bucket, average(hr_stats) FROM hr_1h
WHERE device_id = 'demo-01' AND bucket > now() - INTERVAL '3 days' ORDER BY 1;
SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric,2) mean_ms, round(max_exec_time::numeric,2) max_ms, left(query,80)
FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE query ILIKE '%hr_1h%' ORDER BY calls DESC LIMIT 5;
Client-side p50/p95 in Python:
t=[]
for _ in range(30):
    t0=time.perf_counter(); cur.execute(Q, P); cur.fetchall(); t.append((time.perf_counter()-t0)*1000)
t.sort(); p50=t[len(t)//2]; p95=t[int(0.95*(len(t)-1))]
findings.recommendation:
On the 'Tiger Data' slide, show two numbers side by side and label them:
- 'server execution time' from EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
- 'end-to-end from UTSC to ca-central-1, p50/p95 over 30 warm runs' measured in Python.
Also state the row count scanned and that the data is synthetic. Show the plan lines that prove the claim: only in-range chunks, ColumnarScan on compressed chunks, and far fewer buffers for the cagg. Do not present a single cold or warm run as typical, and do not compare the cagg and raw queries unless both return the same buckets.

findings.topic: 12. Synthetic baseline backfill and demo order
findings.detail:
generate_series(start, stop, step) over timestamptz runs entirely on the server, so there is no network cost (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-srf.html). PointClickCare allows synthetic data, per the brief.
Seven days of heart rate at 1 Hz is about 605 k rows:
INSERT INTO hr_samples (ts, device_id, bpm, source)
SELECT t, 'demo-01', 72 + 8*sin(extract(epoch FROM t)/86400.0*2*pi()) + (random()-0.5)*6, 'synthetic'
FROM generate_series(now() - INTERVAL '7 days', now() - INTERVAL '10 minutes', INTERVAL '1 second') AS t;
Two days of accelerometer data at 50 Hz is about 8.6 M rows (use INTERVAL '20 milliseconds' and the same pattern) and closes at least one 1-day chunk for the compression demo.
Order of steps:
(1) CREATE TABLEs (finding 1).
(2) Create the caggs WITH NO DATA (finding 3).
(3) Run the backfill INSERTs.
(4) CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate for 1m, then 1h, then 1d (finding 5).
(5) Add the refresh, retention and columnstore policies (findings 5, 8, 9).
(6) Run compress_chunk or run_job, then hypertable_columnstore_stats (finding 8).
(7) Start live ingestion with COPY (finding 10).
(8) Show the z-score explanation (finding 7) and the EXPLAIN comparison (finding 11).
findings.recommendation: Tag every synthetic row with source = 'synthetic' and say so on screen. If the 3-day raw retention policy is added in step 5, raw synthetic data older than 3 days is dropped at its next run. The 1-minute aggregates survive because hr_1m's refresh window is only 2 h, so the 7-day baseline remains. Keep the whole sequence in one idempotent migrations.sql, run with psql or an autocommit connection, so it can be rebuilt quickly if the trial service has to be recreated.

bottom_line:
On a current Tiger Cloud trial service (TimescaleDB 2.30.x, Postgres 18 by default, Toolkit preinstalled), every Tiger Data feature the team wants to show can run on one schema. None of the SQL has been run against a live database yet.

1. **Hypertables:** create them with CREATE TABLE ... WITH (tsdb.hypertable, tsdb.partition_column='ts', tsdb.chunk_interval='1 day', tsdb.segmentby='device_id', tsdb.orderby='ts DESC'). This needs 2.20 or later, with automatic partition-column handling from 2.23. It also creates a columnstore policy that compresses after 1 day, with no extra call.
2. **Rollups:** build a 1m -> 1h -> 1d stack of continuous aggregates (2.9 or later). Store stats_agg/time_weight summaries at 1 minute and rollup() them upward. Set timescaledb.materialized_only=false on every layer, because real-time aggregation has been off by default since 2.13. Refresh windows must cover at least two buckets.
3. **Z-score:** compute it with average, stddev and num_vals over stats_agg, against the 7-day baseline from hr_1m, or as a rolling() window over hr_1h. Return its components so the UI can explain the flag. It only moves the next check-in earlier and never escalates.
4. **Columnstore, retention and caggs together:** they coexist if each table's retention is longer than the refresh window of any cagg reading it. A cagg's own columnstore 'after' must be larger than its refresh start_offset. add_columnstore_policy, remove_columnstore_policy and convert_to_columnstore are procedures called with CALL; add_retention_policy and add_continuous_aggregate_policy are functions called with SELECT.
5. **Ingestion:** at about 50 rows/s per device, buffer for 1–2 s and send with psycopg 3 cursor.copy(...FROM STDIN) and write_row, one commit per batch. executemany (pipeline mode, psycopg 3.1+ with libpq 14+) is an acceptable fallback; use unnest + ON CONFLICT if retries can resend samples.
6. **Latency:** pair EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) server time with client-measured p50/p95 over warm runs, and say the data is synthetic.

Skip direct compress (tech preview) and tiering (Scale plan only). Run the version check (finding 0) on the service first.

findings.topic: Outline claim to remove: '48-72 hrs early warning before an acute fall or ER readmission'
findings.detail:
Where it appears: the cheat-sheet row for PointClickCare promises '48-72 hrs early warning before an acute fall or ER readmission', and the narrative says the system stops an ER visit 'days before the fall or collapse happens' (team doc, Outline tab: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vP7VdnVPbzQOYexK0f0syC8p5FPHq4sUg18koOb7zXE/edit?tab=t.o5hhzvs0oeoy).

No source I found supports a 48-72 h horizon from a wearable. The closest evidence works on a scale of weeks or months:
(1) TigerPlace (Phillips et al., West J Nurs Res 2016/17). n=23 residents, 69 falls. Sensor was a ceiling Kinect depth camera, not a wearable. A 7-day cumulative gait-speed decline of 2.54 cm/s gave OR 4.22 for a fall within 3 weeks. A 5.1 cm/s decline gave an 86.3% vs 19.5% probability. The analysis was retrospective at a single site, and the authors call it preliminary (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5272917).
(2) Rantz et al., Gerontology 2015. Bed and motion sensors detected health changes '10 days to 2 weeks' before symptoms, averaged over a one-year pilot (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4444411).
(3) The follow-up RCT: n=171 across 13 assisted-living communities. No significant differences in falls (p=0.12), ER visits or hospitalizations. Nurses often read only the email and skipped the trends (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5679074).
(4) One week of trunk accelerometry raised 6-month fall-prediction AUC from about 0.68 to 0.82. That is a months-ahead risk stratifier (https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/ambulatory-fall-risk-assessment-amount-and-quality-of-daily-life-/).
(5) A review found sensor fall models over-optimistic: only about 15% used prospective falls, and none had external validation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4611882/).
findings.recommendation: Delete the 48-72 h number everywhere: slides, Devpost and the card. Pitch line: 'StillHere flags a change from this resident's own pattern and puts it in front of the nurse with the reasons. In our synthetic scenarios it flagged N days after the scripted onset. That lead time comes from our script, not from evidence. Real-world lead time would need a prospective study.' If you want a literature anchor, cite TigerPlace as 'weeks-scale, camera-based, preliminary'. Don't present it as proof that the scrunchie predicts falls.

findings.topic: Other outline claims care-team judges would find unsupported (and how to reword them)
findings.detail:
Source for each quoted claim: team doc Outline tab (https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vP7VdnVPbzQOYexK0f0syC8p5FPHq4sUg18koOb7zXE/edit?tab=t.o5hhzvs0oeoy).

(a) 'POTS orthostatic intolerance' in senior living. The POTS criteria are a rise of at least 30 bpm with standing held for more than 30 s, plus no orthostatic hypotension, plus chronic symptoms. Most patients present at ages 15-25 and more than 75% are female (HRS 2015, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5267948/). Ruling out OH needs blood pressure, which you don't measure.
(b) 'Orthostatic HR Spike > +28 bpm'. Older adults have a blunted heart-rate response to standing (https://www.benthamscience.com/article/122676). Even beat-to-beat lab equipment has a minimum detectable change of 10.9 bpm at 30 s in older adults (https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/62203/). Apple Watch reports at most about every 5 s (https://support.apple.com/en-us/120277).
(c) 'early UTI/sepsis delirium', 'post-medication over-sedation'. These are diagnoses. LTC surveillance definitions such as McGeer need combinations of findings, including measured temperature (https://spice.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/Respiratory-Tract-Infection-Worksheet-McGeer-SPICE.pdf).
(d) 'Occipital skin temp +0.8 to +1.5 C'. No source given, and the lab hardware can't measure skin temperature (see the temperature finding).
(e) 'Rolling 48-hour deviation from personal baseline'. A 48 h baseline is too short. Day-to-day ICCs for daily sit-to-stand counts in older adults are only 0.63-0.72 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8471908/).
(f) '+35% week-over-week slowing'. No published threshold exists. It is a design parameter.
(g) 'Recommended Action: CNA Orthostatic Vitals & Hydration Check'. In the INTERACT-style workflow, aides observe and report to the nurse (https://www.ohsu.edu/sites/default/files/2019-03/INTERACT-Stop-and-Watch.pdf). 'Hydration' implies a diagnosis of dehydration.
(h) 'Explainable AI Alert Card'. The scoring is rules, so name the AI part precisely.
(i) The Tiger numbers ('<25 ms', '<30 ms', '90%+ compression') need measuring. The docs say 90-98% compression is typical (https://www.tigerdata.com/docs/build/how-to/basic-compression). '4.3 M rows/user/day' is correct arithmetic for 50 Hz (50 x 86,400).
(j) KAZE section: 'Ataxic Sway Index ... signature of CNS depressants/spiking', 'cervical hypotonia' and 'base of the skull is the ultimate biomechanical anchor' are unsourced. The first two are also exactly what the KAZE rules forbid (spiking or incapacitation claims).
findings.recommendation:
Rewording table:
- POTS -> remove.
- 'Orthostatic HR spike' -> 'Heart-rate rise after standing, compared with her usual'.
- UTI/sepsis/delirium/over-sedation -> 'change from her usual pattern: nurse to assess'.
- Skin temperature -> remove from sensing. Optionally show chart temperature as context (no points).
- '48 h baseline' -> 'last 72 h compared with her prior 28 days'.
- '+35%' -> 'demo threshold (configurable)'.
- 'CNA orthostatic vitals & hydration check' -> nurse: 'consider orthostatic vitals per facility protocol'; aide: 'stay with her the first time she stands after resting; tell the nurse about dizziness'.
- 'Explainable AI' -> 'transparent rules + AI-written handoff summary'.
- Tiger numbers -> show your own measured EXPLAIN ANALYZE timing and hypertable stats.
- Strip every spiking/incapacitation term from the KAZE pitch.

findings.topic: Sit-to-stand detection without a gyroscope: what the evidence supports by body location
findings.detail:
Evidence by placement:
- Lower back, IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope). In older adults (test n=11): sensitivity 98%, PPV 86%. The method uses trunk tilt, a wavelet peak and a vertical displacement of at least 0.1 m (Pham 2018, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6104484/).
- Waist, IMU. Healthy older adults reached 100%/100% PPV/sensitivity. Pipeline: vertical acceleration in the global frame, 1.3 Hz low-pass, CWT candidates, a 4 s integration window, a sigmoid fit with R2 > 0.92, and an elevation change of 20-60 cm. The authors needed the gyroscope for orientation and list accelerometer-only operation as future work (Atrsaei 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7271521/).
- Head, accelerometer only. A single tri-axial accelerometer on the mastoid at 100 Hz used head inclination plus changes in the gravity components. It achieved more than 95% accuracy, more than 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity, but in only 12 able-bodied adults (Abdollah 2021, Gait & Posture, https://research.uaeu.ac.ae/en/publications/investigating-the-validity-of-a-single-tri-axial-accelerometer-mo/).
- Pendant (chest), accelerometer only, 50 Hz. Chair-rise detection recall/precision was 85%/87% under protocol but 61%/89% in daily life (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6943965). Feature reliability (peak power, duration) had ICC 0.86-0.93 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4063047/).
- Wrist. I found no validated wrist-only sit-to-stand detector. A search returned only thigh-worn studies (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8471908/).
- Ready-made code: Sit2StandPy is an open-source lower-back accelerometer-only implementation (https://joss.theoj.org/papers/10.21105/joss.02449.pdf).

Engineering judgment (no source): a scrunchie on a swinging ponytail is not rigidly coupled to the head, so it adds pendulum motion to both the transition signal and the sway signal.
findings.recommendation: For senior mode, say 'head-worn (snug bun/clip near the occiput) is our intended placement, based on a 12-person head-accelerometer study; wrist placement is unvalidated'. Expect daily-life recall well below lab figures; the 61% pendant result is the honest benchmark. Every sit-to-stand event must carry a detector_conf. Weekly features must require a minimum event count, so missed events reduce data rather than create false alarms.

findings.topic: Concrete accelerometer-only sit-to-stand algorithm (ADXL345 / LIS3DHTR at 50 Hz) with function names
findings.detail:
Python module senior/sts.py. Main entry: detect_sts_events(acc_g: np.ndarray[N,3], fs: float = 50.0, baro_pa: np.ndarray | None = None, ts: np.ndarray) -> list[StsEvent].

Steps:
(1) Gravity estimate. g_hat = butter_lowpass(acc, 0.5 Hz, order=2, filtfilt). This is the accelerometer-only stand-in for the Kalman orientation that Atrsaei used.
(2) Vertical acceleration. a_v = 9.81 * (dot(acc, g_hat/|g_hat|) - 1.0), then butter_lowpass(a_v, 1.3 Hz). The 1.3 Hz cutoff follows Atrsaei (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7271521/).
(3) Candidates. Use peaks of |sum of CWT coefficients| over scales 0.5-5 s, or a simpler 4 s sliding window, with candidates at least 2 s apart (same paper).
(4) Height change per candidate. Integrate a_v over a 4 s window, remove a linear drift trend (zero velocity at both ends), integrate again to get displacement, then fit a sigmoid. Accept if R2 > 0.92 and the rise is +0.20 to +0.60 m (Atrsaei's gates at L5). A negative result is stand-to-sit.
(5) Supporting head-pitch evidence. Look for a forward pitch dip followed by a return within about 1-3 s, using the head-inclination approach of Abdollah 2021 (https://research.uaeu.ac.ae/en/publications/investigating-the-validity-of-a-single-tri-axial-accelerometer-mo/). The dip size is a tunable you set from your own recordings.
(6) Optional barometer confirmation. See the barometer finding.
(7) Post-stand classification. Label the 60 s after the event as quiet_stand (no step periodicity) or walked_off.

Output fields: StsEvent(ts, dh_m, r2, pitch_dip_deg, baro_dh_m, detector_conf, post_state).

Firmware/bridge: stream raw 50 Hz over the existing USB serial bridge.py. Run detection in the bridge or server, not on the Uno.

Sensor limits: ADXL345 range 1 Hz-3.2 kHz isn't needed; 50-100 Hz is enough. The LIS3DHTR offers 1 Hz-5.3 kHz output data rate and +/-2-16 g ranges (https://www.mouser.lt/pdfDocs/Product_Overview_seeed-studio_Grove_3-Axis_Digital_Accelerometer11.pdf).
findings.recommendation: Build this as the one live senior-mode demo. A judge sits, stands and stays still for 30 s. The bridge posts the event to the API, the event lands on synthetic resident 'B-04', and her card recomputes. Record 20 labelled sit-to-stands and 20 distractors (bending to pick something up, nodding, sitting down) from the team tonight. Tune the gates on those recordings and report the confusion matrix on the Devpost. Don't quote the literature's accuracy as yours.

findings.topic: Repurpose the MLH 'Grove Temperature and Barometer Sensor' as a height-change sensor for standing up
findings.detail:
What the MLH hardware lab lists: 'Grove Temperature and Barometer Sensor (3)' and 'Grove 3 Axis Digital Accelerometer (10)'. There is no heart-rate sensor or thermistor (https://guide.mlh.com/organizer-resources/hardware-lab-contents).

Two Seeed boards fit that name:
- Grove BMP280: +/-1 hPa absolute accuracy (https://learn.pakronics.com.au/seed-studio/grove-modules/sensors/grove-barometer_sensor-bmp280). The Bosch BMP280 has relative accuracy of +/-0.12 hPa, which Bosch equates to about +/-1 m (so about 12 Pa per m), RMS noise of 1.3 Pa, and a temperature offset coefficient of 1.5 Pa/K, about 12.6 cm/K (https://forums.parallax.com/uploads/editor/gm/8y6uzm9khhil.pdf).
- Grove SPA06-003: relative accuracy +/-0.03 hPa (+/-0.25 m), resolution 0.06 Pa, temperature +/-1 C. Library Seeed_Arduino_SPA06; class SPL07_003 with spl.readPressure() (Pa), spl.readTemperature() (C), spl.calcAltitude(); I2C address 0x77 (https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/grove_barometer_sensor_spa06_003/).

Precedent for this use: a trunk-worn barometer distinguished sit-to-stand transitions from stationary postures with 99.5% accuracy (4.16 s averaging, 7 healthy adults) (https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/189787?ln=fr). A pendant combining accelerometer and barometer was used to detect and assess sit-to-stand in 119 older people (https://repositum.tuwien.at/handle/20.500.12708/3590).

My estimate: a 0.4-0.6 m head rise is about 5-7 Pa. That is marginal for the BMP280 and workable for the SPA06-003 if you average windows.
findings.recommendation: Read the chip marking on the borrowed board. Use it as the barometer, not as a thermometer. Function: baro_height_change(p_pa, ts, t_event) = -(median(p[t+3..t+13 s]) - median(p[t-13..t-3 s])) / 12.0, in metres. Count it as confirmation when the value is +0.25 m or more. Re-zero after the device is put on, because body heat drifts about 1.5 Pa/K on the BMP280. Treat door slams and HVAC pressure steps as noise: require agreement with the accelerometer. If the chip is a BMP280 and the signal is too noisy, drop the barometer and say so.

findings.topic: Apple Watch heart rate via HeartCast: what it can and cannot give senior mode
findings.detail:
Sampling: Apple says Series 12 and Ultra 4 measure 'as often as every five seconds, even when you're in motion' (https://support.apple.com/en-us/120277).

HeartCast: its listing says it broadcasts heart rate over Bluetooth to nearby equipment once you press Start on watch and phone. It doesn't state a broadcast rate, and a user review reports irregular update intervals (https://apps.apple.com/app/id1499771124).

Battery: workout tracking lasts up to 10 h on Series 12 and 7 h on SE 3. All-day battery is up to 24 h and 18 h respectively (https://www.apple.com/watch/battery/). That rules out continuous 24/7 broadcasting and makes overnight heart rate impractical for a resident.

What the published orthostatic heart-rate work used: TILDA's heart-rate recovery result came from beat-to-beat Finometer data, binned in 10 s intervals (https://www.tara.tcd.ie/items/6f35a541-297f-48be-8cad-63f0dd78948e). That resolution can't be reproduced from about 5 s smoothed watch values.

Heart rate alone is a poor stand-up detector. The usual rise is small and blunted with age (https://www.benthamscience.com/article/122676), and it sits within the 10.9 bpm minimum detectable change (https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/62203/).
findings.recommendation: Use heart rate only as a response measured around accelerometer-detected stand-ups, never as the trigger. In the Chrome Web Bluetooth page, stamp each 0x2A37 notification with Date.now() on arrival and POST batches to /senior/ingest/hr. Compute features at 5 s resolution. Require at least 6 heart-rate samples in [t-60, t] and at least 8 in [t, t+60]; otherwise set hr_* to NULL with reason='hr_coverage'. In the pitch: 'live HR during the demo; resident histories use synthetic HR'. Show HR coverage on the card.

findings.topic: Normal heart-rate response to standing in older adults, and the 'orthostatic recovery' features to compute
findings.detail:
What normal looks like:
- In healthy people the initial heart-rate response to standing is usually bimodal and happens within about 30 s. With age the heart-rate response attenuates (Current Aging Science 2022 review, https://www.benthamscience.com/article/122676).
- Older adults with orthostatic hypotension lacked the early heart-rate peak and had a smaller, slower rise over the first 40 s (https://eprints.lib.hokudai.ac.jp/repo/huscap/all/8425/ANS.pdf).
- Sit-to-stand produces smaller heart-rate increases than lie-to-stand, and older adults show a blunted heart-rate response (AJP-Regu 2026, doi 10.1152/ajpregu.00019.2026, https://www.citedrive.com/en/discovery/gravitational-load-sex-and-age-sex-effects-on-cardiovascular-compensatory-responses-during-sit-to-stand-and-lie-to-stand-transitions/).

Why recovery speed is a reasonable thing to track:
- TILDA (n=4,475, age 50+, active stand from lying): each 1 bpm slower heart-rate recovery 10-20 s after standing raised mortality hazard by 6% (https://www.tara.tcd.ie/items/6f35a541-297f-48be-8cad-63f0dd78948e).
- Frailty was linked to slower BP and heart-rate recovery. Among frailty criteria, only slow gait speed was consistently related (https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/274093).
- Older adults sway about 2.5x more than young adults in the stabilization phase right after sit-to-stand (12.38 vs 4.98; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7161000/).

Measurement noise: the minimum detectable change in heart rate at 30 s is 10.9 bpm (https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/62203/).
findings.recommendation:
Function compute_orthostatic_response(event, hr, acc) -> dict. Fields:
- hr_base = median HR over [t-60, t-5] s
- hr_delta_30 = median HR over [t+25, t+35] s minus hr_base
- hr_settle_s = first time after the peak at which the 10 s rolling median stays within +/-5 bpm of median HR over [t+45, t+60] s; censored at 60
- sway_settle_s = first 2 s window after which the RMS of 0.1-3.5 Hz horizontal acceleration stays below 1.25 x her quiet-stand RMS for 3 windows; NULL if walked_off

Compare weekly medians with at least 5 events against her 28-day baseline with at least 15 events. Treat changes in hr_delta_30 under 11 bpm as noise. Call it 'inspired by' TILDA, never 'validated'.

findings.topic: Defensible non-diagnostic wording: orthostatic hypotension is defined by blood pressure
findings.detail:
Definitions:
- Orthostatic hypotension: a fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or at least 10 mmHg diastolic, or lightheadedness or dizziness. CDC STEADI protocol: lie down 5 min, measure BP and pulse, stand, repeat at 1 and 3 min (https://www.cdc.gov/steadi/media/pdfs/STEADI-Assessment-MeasuringBP-508.pdf). Consensus source: Freeman et al., Clin Auton Res 2011;21:69-72 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21431947/).
- POTS also requires the absence of orthostatic hypotension, so it is a blood-pressure-dependent call too (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/5267948/).

Regulatory language (US):
- FDA's January 2026 General Wellness guidance lets notifications count as wellness only if they don't name a disease, don't call the output abnormal or diagnostic, don't include clinical thresholds or treatment recommendations, and don't provide ongoing alerts to manage a condition (https://www.foley.com/p/102meea/digital-health-policy-fda-relaxes-restrictions-over-wearables-and-ai-decision-ma/).
- Non-device CDS must not analyze 'a pattern or signal from a signal acquisition system', and must let the clinician independently review the basis for a recommendation (https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2026/2026-01-20-automation-bias-and-clinical-practice-fda-makes-incremental-updates-to-clinical-decision-support-software-guidance). A staff alert driven by your sensor signals therefore falls outside both safe harbours.
findings.recommendation:
Card template, to copy as is: 'Change from her usual: after standing up this week, her heart rate and balance took longer to settle (median 41 s vs her usual 27 s; 11 stand-ups). Heart rate alone cannot show whether her blood pressure drops on standing. Suggested next step (nurse): consider lying/standing BP and pulse per facility protocol, and ask about dizziness.'

Blocklist for any generated text: hypotension, POTS, dehydrat*, UTI, sepsis, infection, delirium, diagnos*, predict*, 'will fall'.

Footer on every card: 'Hackathon prototype, synthetic data, not a medical device, not clinically validated.'

findings.topic: Evidence that gait/sway change predicts falls, and how to measure it with the scrunchie
findings.detail:
Evidence that exists:
- Daily-life trunk accelerometry improves fall-risk ranking over a 6-month horizon (https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/ambulatory-fall-risk-assessment-amount-and-quality-of-daily-life-/). Over 1 year, AUC was 0.66-0.72 for time to first fall (https://ideas.repec.org/a/plo/pone00/0158623.html).
- A meta-analysis of quiet-standing centre-of-pressure measures (44 studies, 7,176 older adults) found that sway area per unit time and mean velocity discriminate fallers (https://centreborelli.ens-paris-saclay.fr/en/node/484).
- Within-person change: TigerPlace linked a 7-day in-home gait-speed decline to falls within 3 weeks (camera-based, n=23, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5272917).

Caveats: inertial-sensor fall models report accuracy of 62-100% and mostly use retrospective faller labels (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3751184/). The literature is over-optimistic (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4611882/).

Can the borrowed hardware resolve sway?
- Quiet-stance trunk RMS acceleration at L5 was 0.052-0.073 m/s2 in controls and about 0.09-0.11 m/s2 in Parkinson's (50 Hz, 3.5 Hz low-pass; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3481400/).
- ADXL345 noise is under 1.0 LSB rms (x/y) at 100 Hz, with 3.9 mg/LSB at +/-2 g, i.e. under about 0.038 m/s2 rms before filtering (https://pdf.direnc.net/upload/adxl345.pdf).
- My calculation: low-passing to 3.5 Hz cuts white noise by about sqrt(3.5/50), roughly 0.26x, which makes it usable.
findings.recommendation:
Use a gait_daily table with these features: sts_count, walking_bouts, cadence_cv (step-interval coefficient of variation from vertical-acceleration autocorrelation), sway_rms_quiet (0.1-3.5 Hz, only in quiet-stand segments of at least 10 s), and wear_hours.

Rule: current = mean of the last 72 h; baseline = the prior 28 days. Compute a robust z = (current - median) / (1.4826 x MAD). Score 1 point at z >= 2 and 2 points at z >= 3. Require at least 2 of 3 days present.

Pitch it as 'mobility looks different from her usual', not 'fall predicted'.

findings.topic: Skin temperature: not feasible with the lab hardware; drop it from sensing (optionally show chart temperature as context)
findings.detail:
Hardware: the only temperature-capable part in the MLH lab is the 'Grove Temperature and Barometer Sensor' (https://guide.mlh.com/organizer-resources/hardware-lab-contents). Its temperature reading is +/-1 C (https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/grove_barometer_sensor_spa06_003/), and it is mounted on a PCB inside an enclosure, so it reads air/board temperature, not skin. The LIS3DHTR's 'integrated temperature sensor' is likewise on-chip (https://www.mouser.lt/pdfDocs/Product_Overview_seeed-studio_Grove_3-Axis_Digital_Accelerometer11.pdf). A +/-1 C sensor cannot resolve the outline's +0.8 C threshold.

Physiology: skin temperature tracks core poorly. Forehead read about 0.5 C below oral/axillary, with r = 0.07-0.26 against core sites, across ambient 14-32 C (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9740153/).

What LTC fever surveillance actually uses (revised McGeer): single oral temperature > 37.8 C, repeated oral > 37.2 C, repeated rectal > 37.5 C, or > 1.1 C above baseline from any site (https://spice.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/Respiratory-Tract-Infection-Worksheet-McGeer-SPICE.pdf). These are body-site measurements, not nape skin. I found no source for the outline's '+0.8 to +1.5 C occipital' range.
findings.recommendation: Drop occipital skin temperature from the sensor list and the risk score. If you want a temperature line on the card, take it from a synthetic chart_vitals table ('Chart: 37.9 C at 06:10, entered by RN (synthetic)'). Show it as context with 0 points. That also fits PointClickCare's 'unify existing data' angle (team doc ideation tab). Say plainly on the Devpost: 'The lab sensor measures air temperature; we did not fake a skin-temperature signal.'

findings.topic: Nocturnal restlessness: some evidence, but simulate it
findings.detail:
Evidence: a systematic review of 14 studies (315 patients) found that delirious patients had higher night-time activity, lower sleep efficiency and a smaller day-night activity difference (Davoudi et al., Crit Care Explor 2019, https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10213929). These were mostly hospital studies with wrist or thigh devices, and the evidence base is limited.

Why it can't be measured live here: Apple Watch workout-mode battery (10 h on Series 12) rules out overnight HeartCast (https://www.apple.com/watch/battery/). A hair-worn device during sleep is impractical (my judgment).

Framing: Rantz's sensor program used a bed sensor for 'restlessness' (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4444411), so 'night-time movement higher than usual' is a defensible change-of-condition signal. It is not a delirium detector.
findings.recommendation: Make it a synthetic-only feature in a night_summary table (restlessness_index = minutes with wrist-acceleration activity counts above threshold between 23:00 and 06:00, divided by wear minutes). Rule: robust z >= 2 on 2 consecutive nights scores 1 point. A single bad night scores 0, which is one of the scripted counter-examples. Card wording: 'More movement at night than usual (2 nights).'

findings.topic: Designing the explainable alert card for care staff
findings.detail:
Precedents to borrow from:
- NEWS2 scores each parameter 0-3, sums to an aggregate, and ties aggregate tiers to response levels (0-4 low; a single parameter scoring 3 is low-medium; 5-6 medium; 7+ high). This makes the score explainable by construction (https://www.rcp.ac.uk/media/2acdezkd/news2-chart-2_news-thresholds-and-triggers_0.pdf).
- Alert fatigue: busy clinicians become desensitized to alerts. The fix is to tier by severity, interrupt only for the most severe, and drop inconsequential alerts (https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/alert-fatigue).
- Front-line workflow: INTERACT Stop and Watch has aides circle an observed change and notify a nurse or supervisor. Its licence says it 'may not be resold or incorporated in software without permission of Florida Atlantic University' (https://www.ohsu.edu/sites/default/files/2019-03/INTERACT-Stop-and-Watch.pdf).
- SBAR is IHI's standard structure for handoffs (https://www.ihi.org/resources/Pages/Tools/SBARToolkit.aspx).
- Clinician trust in ML hinges on explanations clinicians can check (Tonekaboni 2019, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v106/tonekaboni19a.html).
- In the Rantz RCT, nurses often read only the short email and skipped trend views (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5679074). So the card itself must carry the explanation.
findings.recommendation:
Card layout, top to bottom:
1. Banner: 'SYNTHETIC DATA - prototype'.
2. Resident (fictional ID) and tier chip: No change / Watch / Nurse review today.
3. One-line headline.
4. 'Why flagged' table, one row per rule: what changed | this period (value, n, dates) | her usual (value, n, dates) | change | points.
5. 'Checked, not flagged' rows.
6. Data quality: wear hours, HR coverage, events detected.
7. Limits line: 'HR alone can't show BP; not a diagnosis'.
8. Suggested next step, split into Nurse and Aide.
9. Sparkline per flagged metric.
10. Buttons: Acknowledge / Assessed - no change / Vitals taken / Escalated, stored as feedback.

Only 'Nurse review today' sends a Telegram push; 'Watch' stays on the dashboard. Don't reproduce the Stop and Watch form or acronym. Say 'fits facilities' existing change-of-condition workflow'.

findings.topic: Replace the opaque 0-100 risk score with transparent points (and keep a 0-100 view only if you must)
findings.detail:
Rationale: NEWS2 shows that summed per-parameter points can be read at a glance and tied to actions (https://www.rcp.ac.uk/media/2acdezkd/news2-chart-2_news-thresholds-and-triggers_0.pdf). The CDS criterion that the clinician must be able to independently review the basis also favours visible arithmetic (https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2026/2026-01-20-automation-bias-and-clinical-practice-fda-makes-incremental-updates-to-clinical-decision-support-software-guidance).

Proposed rules. All thresholds are invented demo parameters, stored in a rule_config table and shown on the Devpost.
- R1 stand-up settle time (hr_settle_s, or sway_settle_s if no HR). Weekly median vs 28-day median: +25% -> 1, +35% -> 2, +50% -> 3. Also needs an absolute change of at least 8 s, at least 5 events and at least 15 baseline events.
- R2 heart-rate rise after standing. |change in median hr_delta_30| >= 11 bpm -> 1. The 11 bpm floor is the measurement noise from https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/62203/. Suppressed if resident.on_rate_control_med (context: heart-rate response is not interpretable there).
- R3 mobility drift (72 h vs 28 d, robust z): z >= 2 -> 1, z >= 3 -> 2.
- R4 night-time movement on 2 consecutive nights: z >= 2 -> 1.
- Data gate: if wear_hours_7d < 40, or R1 has fewer than 5 events, show 'Not enough data', never 'low risk'.

Tiers: 0-1 No change; 2-3 Watch; 4 or more, or any single 3, Nurse review today. If the UI needs 0-100, show round(100 x points/max_points) next to the points, never alone.
findings.recommendation: Implement as pure Python: score_resident(resident_id, as_of) -> Card. It reads the continuous aggregates below and writes alert_card rows. Unit-test each rule against the synthetic counter-examples: a beta-blocker start should not reach 'Nurse review today' on R2 alone, and a single bad night should score 0.

findings.topic: 'Use of AI' for PointClickCare: LLM writes the handoff from the rule JSON only (Vultr Serverless Inference)
findings.detail:
Endpoint: Vultr's OpenAI-compatible API, base_url https://api.vultrinference.com/v1. POST https://api.vultrinference.com/v1/chat/completions with 'Authorization: Bearer <VULTR_SERVERLESS_INFERENCE_API_KEY>'. The model list is at https://api.vultrinference.com/v1/chat/models (https://docs.vultr.com/how-to-use-vultr-serverless-inference-in-python and https://docs.vultr.com/how-to-use-vultr-serverless-inference-in-nodejs).

Automation bias is now an explicit concern in the FDA's 2026 CDS guidance (https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2026/2026-01-20-automation-bias-and-clinical-practice-fda-makes-incremental-updates-to-clinical-decision-support-software-guidance). That argues for keeping the decision in the rules and the language in the LLM.

findings.topic: Synthetic multi-day resident data generator: honest design (N residents x D days, scripted declines and counter-examples)
findings.detail:
Precedent: Synthea builds 'realistic, but absolutely not real' patients from published statistics and modular disease logic (Walonoski et al., JAMIA 2018; https://www.mitre.org/news-insights/impact-story/synthetic-patient-records-help-deliver-real-health-outcomes and https://docs.bcbi.brown.edu/codiac-for-health/ursa-ri/datasets/syntheticmass). The PointClickCare track says synthetic data does not count against you (team doc).

Where the trait ranges come from:
- sway_rms_quiet 0.05-0.11 m/s2, from Mancini (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3481400/).
- Day-to-day noise on sts_count: ICC 0.63-0.72 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8471908/).
- Blunted heart-rate response with age (https://www.benthamscience.com/article/122676).

Loader: use psycopg 3 COPY. with cur.copy('COPY stand_event (ts, resident_id, ...) FROM STDIN') as cp: cp.write_row(row) (https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/basic/copy.html).
findings.recommendation:
Module sim/generate.py.

Functions:
- make_cohort(n_residents=12, n_days=42, seed=11) -> list[Resident]
- assign_scenarios(cohort, rng)
- simulate_day(res, day, state, rng) -> DayData
- write_to_db(conn, cohort, days)
- evaluate(conn, as_of) -> Report

Resident traits: age 75-95, hr_rest 58-85, on_rate_control_med, uses_walker, settle_base_s 15-35, sts_per_day 8-25, sway_rms_quiet 0.05-0.11.

Scenarios. Use days 0-27 as baseline and 28-41 as the test period.
- stable (at least half the cohort)
- gradual_mobility_decline: sway +3%/day and sts_per_day -3%/day from onset
- slower_settling: settle time +5%/day for 7 days
- clustered_change: R1 + R3 + 2 restless nights

Counter-examples:
- beta_blocker_start: HR rise is blunted, mobility unchanged
